title: Your Wallet Was Not Designed for Lao Kip
summary: Lao kip comes in huge denominations and ATMs cap you at small withdrawals with real fees. Here is how LAO QR and a travel wallet let you skip most of that in Vientiane and Luang Prabang.
body_markdown:
Change a couple hundred dollars into Lao kip and you will understand immediately why this article exists. The kip comes in enormous denominations, tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands per note, and a note that sounds like a fortune might cover one iced coffee. By day two your wallet does not close anymore. By day four you have a rubber band around a brick of paper.


That bulk problem would be merely funny if getting the cash were easy. It is not. Laos is one of the more expensive countries in Southeast Asia to withdraw money in, not because things cost a lot, but because of how the ATMs are set up.


## The ATM math that catches everyone


Here is the trap. ATMs in Laos tend to have low per-withdrawal limits. Each withdrawal carries a local machine fee, and your home bank often adds its own foreign ATM fee and a currency markup on top. Because the limit per transaction is low, you cannot do one big withdrawal and spread the fixed fees across it. You end up doing several small withdrawals, and paying the full stack of fees every single time.


Travelers who breeze through Thailand or Vietnam on a couple of ATM runs arrive in Laos and find themselves queuing at machines every other day, feeding fees into the system each time, and still walking around with that brick of kip.


One more thing while you are standing at the machine: if the screen offers to charge you in your home currency instead of kip, decline it. That is dynamic currency conversion, and the rate baked into it is almost never in your favor. Always choose kip if you do withdraw.


## LAO QR changed the picture, quietly


While visitors were busy hunting ATMs, locals largely stopped carrying cash for everyday purchases. Laos has a national QR standard called LAO QR, and in Vientiane and Luang Prabang it has spread fast. The coffee shop near Patuxai, the minimart, the restaurant along the Mekong, the stall at the Luang Prabang night market with the printed code taped to the table, they all take it.


Watch locals pay and you will see the routine: open a banking app like BCEL OnePay, scan the merchant's code, type the amount, show the confirmation screen. No change counted, no crumpled notes. The merchant glances at the phone, nods, done.


The catch for visitors has always been that those apps want a Lao bank account, which you do not have and are not going to open for a two-week trip.


## How a visitor joins in without a Lao bank


This is exactly the gap a travel wallet like Moreta Pay fills. You top up the wallet before or during your trip from your own bank at home, via a US bank connection, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer, or an international card, all in your own currency. Then in Laos you scan the same LAO QR codes the locals scan.


The flow at the counter takes a few seconds. Scan the merchant's code, check the merchant name and the amount, look at the exchange rate shown on screen, confirm. The wallet converts to kip at that moment and the merchant is paid instantly in their own currency. No foreign transaction fee hiding on a statement weeks later, no guessing what rate you got. The rate is right there before you tap confirm, which is more than any ATM in Laos will ever show you.


In practice this means a dinner in Vientiane, a guesthouse bill in Luang Prabang, groceries, a coffee, a massage, all paid from your phone, with your kip brick staying untouched in your bag.


## Where you still want paper kip


Do not go fully cashless in Laos. Not yet. The QR coverage is strong in the two main tourist cities and growing elsewhere, but it thins out fast once you leave them.


Keep cash for these situations:


- Tuk tuks and songthaews, which are negotiated and paid in cash almost everywhere.


- Rural areas, small villages, and stops along the slow boat route, where phone signal itself can be patchy.


- Tiny purchases from older vendors who never printed a code, a bag of fruit, a sticky rice basket at the morning market.


- Temple donations and entrance fees at smaller sites.


This mirrors the pattern across the region, where


[micro-fares and informal transport are the last holdout for cash](https://moretapay.com/blog/the-jeepney-and-tricycle-problem-why-cash-still-wins-over-qr-for-micro-fares)


even in countries where QR dominates everything else. Laos is no different, just a few steps earlier on the same curve.


The practical move: make one deliberate withdrawal or currency exchange for your cash buffer, accept the fee on that single transaction, and cover everything else by QR. One fee instead of eight is the whole game.


## A one-week Laos money plan


Putting it together, here is what a week split between Vientiane and Luang Prabang can look like:


**Before you fly:**


top up your Moreta Pay wallet from your home bank while you are still on good wifi. Doing it in advance means you land ready to pay, not ready to queue.


**Day one:**


get your cash buffer. One withdrawal, or exchange some cash you brought. Think tuk tuk money and market snacks, not your whole budget.


**Daily:**


default to scanning. Cafes, restaurants, minimarts, your guesthouse, laundry service. If you see a QR code displayed, try it. Worst case, the vendor shakes their head and you use cash.


**Booking ahead:**


QR payment also works for online platforms like Agoda and Trip.com that support QR checkout, useful for locking in the next guesthouse while you are on the bus.


**Leaving:**


this is the quiet bonus. Leftover wallet balance is not leftover kip. Nobody wants to re-exchange a stack of Lao notes at the border, but a wallet balance just comes with you to the next country. If Thailand is your next stop, the


[same approach works with PromptPay](https://moretapay.com/blog/thailand-avoid-atm-fees-bad-exchange-rates-promptpay-qr-2026-2026-10-10)


the moment you cross.


Laos rewards travelers who slow down, and it punishes travelers who do not plan their money. The ATM fees, the withdrawal limits, the wallet full of paper, all of it is avoidable now that LAO QR is on the counters of Vientiane and Luang Prabang.
